notes:
Zero turns start in this stretch. The fragment contains no bold run at all: it is one continuous speech running from before the fragment's first character to past its last. Checked against data/raw/senado/taquigraficas/2002-02-21_r83_ORDINARIA.html for context only: the last speaker label before this stretch is 'Sr. Alfonsin. --' (printed with the accent) and the next bold label after the stretch ends is far downstream, so the whole fragment is that one senator's continuing floor speech. I did not list it, per rule 1. EVENTS: empty, and deliberately so. The fragment contains two parenthesised audience notes, and I first recorded both. On the corpus convention - an event is a note printed as its OWN paragraph, while an italic fragment inline inside a speaker's paragraph is merged back into that speech rather than splitting the turn (the PDF side calls this block type inline_italic) - I checked where each one actually sits on the page, and BOTH are inline, so both were reclassified as speech and the list is empty. - '(Risas.)' in the markup, printing '(Risas.)', with only the word and its stop italic and the parentheses roman. It sits mid-paragraph: '...queridos companeros... --companeros, correligionarios y colegas--. (Risas.) Creo que esto es lo urgente.' The same

continues after it in the same voice. - '(risas).' in the markup, printing '(risas).', with the whole thing italic, lowercased, and the full stop pushed outside the closing parenthesis. It too sits mid-sentence: '...lo que me dolio fue lo de la vejez (risas). Y que ademas de esa jubilacion contaba con lo que ganaba en el Senado.' Neither was judged unreal - laughter was audibly recorded by the stenographer in both places. They are simply not standalone event paragraphs, so under the convention they belong to Alfonsin's own paragraphs and do not split his turn. I have kept both typesettings recorded verbatim above, because the second is a typist's botch of the same note and a maintainer should be able to see that the page prints the identical event two different ways. Three other italic runs in the fragment are NOT events and I deliberately left them out: 'post mortem' and 'staff' are foreign-language words italicised inside the senator's own sentences ('las soluciones siempre llegan post mortem', 'le daban hasta el staff'). They are spoken text, not stenographer's notes: they carry no opening dash, sit mid-sentence, and are grammatically part of the surrounding speech. A rule that treats every run as an event would wrongly harvest these. The reclassification of the two laughter notes above is that same distinction drawn one level finer: not italic-versus-roman but standalone-paragraph-versus-inline. In this fragment every single italic run, laughter included, turns out to be inline, so nothing here is an event. No headings, no section numbers and no furniture (no back-links, no contents entries, no sign-off) appear in this fragment. Every

here opens a body paragraph of the same speech; none of them starts a turn.
